questions.q: Why does Briarcliff's design use time-based scheduled actions instead of an approval process?
options: Approval processes are faster than scheduled actions
The problem is a pure countdown to a deadline -- nobody needs to approve or reject anything
Scheduled actions don't require a trigger record
Approval processes can't send emails
questions.explain: Unlike the quote approval case study, this scenario has no decision for a person to make -- just a deadline to track.

questions.q: Why does the SLA warning fire at the three-hour mark instead of right at the four-hour deadline?
options: Three hours is a Salesforce system limit
It fires at three hours purely by coincidence
So the customer is notified earlier
To give the case owner a real window to act before a manager is notified
questions.explain: Paging someone the instant a case is created would train staff to ignore the warning -- the one-hour buffer gives them time to actually respond.

questions.q: What happens to the four-hour breach notification if the case is closed before the deadline?
options: It never fires -- the scheduled action depends on the case still being open
It still fires but is marked as resolved
It fires but is sent to the customer only
It fires immediately when the case is closed
questions.explain: The breach step's condition checks that the case is still open; closing it in time removes the pending scheduled action.

questions.q: In the design, who is notified at T+0 if the case is still open?
options: Only the customer
No one -- only the T-1 hour warning sends a notification
The case owner's manager, with the case also flagged as escalated and the customer emailed
The Salesforce system administrator
questions.explain: The breach step reaches a different, more senior audience than the earlier warning, plus a field update and customer email.

questions.q: What was support leadership's original complaint at Briarcliff, before any automation was designed?
options: SLA breaches were discovered only when the customer called to complain, not before
Cases were being closed too quickly
The SLA target was set too low
Case owners were overloaded with warnings
questions.explain: There was no internal warning system, so breaches went unnoticed internally until a customer raised the issue.
